analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Energy Department's public-interest review of natural gas exports and requires automatic approval.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 224-200 on February 15, 2024, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a company that wants to ship liquefied natural gas (LNG) to other countries must get permission from the Department of Energy, which weighs whether exports serve the public interest — including effects on prices and supply at home. This bill deletes that test. It moves the decision to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which handles terminal construction permits, and requires FERC to treat every export application as automatically in the public interest. In practice, no regulator could say no to an export application on public-interest grounds.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies building and operating LNG export terminals, and the natural gas producers that supply them, gain a fast, near-automatic path to export approvals. Foreign buyers of US gas also gain. The bill preserves presidential authority to block exports to sanctioned countries, but for everyone else, approval would no longer hinge on any weighing of effects on American consumers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the sections of the Natural Gas Act that require Department of Energy approval for natural gas imports and exports, including the provisions tied to free trade agreements [S4].

It gives FERC the exclusive authority to approve export and import facilities, including LNG terminals, and requires FERC to deem the export or import of natural gas consistent with the public interest — removing any case-by-case public-interest judgment [S4].
For terminal developers, this means one regulator instead of two and no discretionary hurdle at the export stage, shortening and de-risking the permitting process [S4].
The bill preserves the President's authority to prohibit exports under sanctions and emergency laws, including against state sponsors of terrorism [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses that heat homes and power factories with natural gas would bear the risk of higher domestic prices, since exporting more gas links US prices to higher world markets. The public also loses the only stage where a federal agency weighs exports against domestic supply, price, and climate effects, because the bill mandates that exports be deemed in the public interest. Communities near terminals lose a federal check on siting decisions beyond FERC's existing process.

drawbacks.text: The bill orders FERC to deem exports consistent with the public interest, so the approval process could no longer consider whether shipping gas abroad raises costs or strains supply for American consumers and utilities [S4].

Currently DOE authorizes exports and weighs the public interest; the bill repeals that review and consolidates the decision in FERC, which under the bill could not deny an application on public-interest grounds [S2].

Moving more US gas to world markets tends to push domestic natural gas prices toward higher international levels, a cost that lands on heating bills, electricity rates, and manufacturers that use gas as a feedstock.

Even supporters of LNG exports acknowledged in debate that the bill was a response to the administration's pause on export decisions; an automatic-approval mandate is a blunt instrument that removes regulators' ability to weigh trade-offs rather than speed up a fair review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real benefit — faster, more predictable permitting for export terminals and more US gas sold abroad — comes at the cost of eliminating the only case-by-case public-interest check on exports. Because it mandates approval rather than merely speeding review, the costs to domestic gas consumers are locked in with no offsetting safeguard. A narrower bill that set deadlines for DOE decisions would have addressed permitting delays without removing the review altogether.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a party-line vote in February 2024, but the Senate never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 31, 2024, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1].
It never received a committee markup; instead, the Rules Committee advanced a closed rule, and the House debated and voted on it about two weeks after introduction [S6].

A Democratic motion to recommit the bill to committee — a last-chance attempt to send it back for changes — failed 209-213, with 209 of 212 voting Democrats in favor and all 213 voting Republicans opposed [S7].
The House passed the bill 224-200 on February 15, 2024: 215 of 219 voting Republicans voted yes, and only 9 of 212 voting Democrats joined them [S8].
The Senate never considered the bill — no Senate committee referral, vote, or floor action appears in its action history [S6].
The bill died on January 3, 2025, when the 118th Congress ended, without becoming law [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the Energy Department kept its authority to weigh LNG export applications against the public interest, and exporters did not get the automatic approvals the bill promised. Domestic gas consumers retained that check; exporters and terminal developers went without the change they sought.

for.name: 215 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, 215-0 among those voting

against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage, 200-9 among those voting

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the Senate took no action on it

against.name: President Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: Ordered a pause on new LNG export permit decisions in January 2024, which the bill was drafted to undo

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 215 of 219 voting Republicans voted yes, while only 9 of 212 voting Democrats joined them; the Democratic motion to recommit failed 209-213 along the same lines.

industries.note: The bill removes the Energy Department's public-interest test and requires FERC to deem every export application in the public interest, clearing the main discretionary hurdle to building and operating export terminals. Their gain comes at the risk of higher domestic gas prices and the loss of a federal check on exports.

Automatic export approvals would expand the market for US gas at higher world prices. More exports tend to pull domestic prices upward, so the industry's gain in this bill runs against household heating and electricity costs.

These businesses use natural gas as a fuel and feedstock and would face the same upward price pressure from expanded exports that households would, with the public-interest review that weighs their interests deleted.
